blocks.content: EARLY NATIONALIST / MODERATE PHASE

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The year 1885 marked a turning point in Indian history with the establishment of the Indian National Congress.
The Moderate Phase (1885–1905) relied on peaceful, constitutional agitation focused on prayers, petitions, and protests.
Dadabhai Naoroji highlighted economic exploitation through the 'Drain of Wealth' theory.
Key demands included legislative expansion, administrative Indianization, and reduced military spending.
The British government initially tolerated the INC but soon became hostile, with Lord Dufferin labeling it a 'microscopic minority'.

blocks.content: 1. Introduction: Why 1885–1905 is a Turning Point

The period from 1885 to 1905 marks the beginning of the organised Indian National Movement. Before 1885, resistance against British rule was largely local, unorganised, and limited in scope. With the formation of the Indian National Congress (INC) in 1885, Indian nationalism acquired an all-India character. This phase is called the Early Nationalist or Moderate Phase because the leaders believed in peaceful, constitutional, and legal methods of struggle. Although this phase did not achieve immediate political freedom, it played a decisive role in politically awakening the Indian people and laying the foundation for later mass movements.
2. Background: Growth of Indian National Consciousness
Indian nationalism did not emerge suddenly. It was the result of several long-term developments under British rule which created a sense of unity and shared grievances among Indians.

British conquest unified India under one administrative system for the first time. Uniform laws, administration, and centralized authority unknowingly helped Indians realise that they were part of a single political unit.

Western education introduced ideas of liberty, equality, democracy, nationalism, and rule of law. Educated Indians began comparing British ideals with British practices in India, leading to political awareness and criticism of colonial rule.
Newspapers such as Kesari, Amrita Bazar Patrika, The Hindu, and Bengalee played a vital role in spreading nationalist ideas and exposing British policies.
British economic policies led to poverty, famines, unemployment, and decline of Indian industries. These conditions made Indians conscious of the exploitative nature of colonial rule.
Indians faced racial discrimination in administration, army, judiciary, and public life. Events like the Ilbert Bill controversy exposed British racial arrogance.
3. Formation of Indian National Congress (1885)
The Indian National Congress was founded in December 1885 as a platform for educated Indians to discuss political problems and present their demands to the British government.

A.O. Hume, a retired British civil servant, played a key role in founding the INC. He believed that the Congress would act as a ‘safety valve’ to channel Indian discontent into constitutional methods.
Why 1885–1905 is a Turning Point
The first session of the INC was held in Bombay in 1885. It was presided over by W.C. Bonnerjee and attended by 72 delegates from different parts of India.
4. The Moderates (1885–1905): Ideology and Beliefs
The leaders of this phase are known as Moderates because they believed in moderation, gradual reforms, and cooperation with the British.
Moderates believed that British rule was ultimately beneficial and could be reformed. They trusted British liberal traditions and expected justice through petitions and dialogue.
Dadabhai Naoroji, Gopal Krishna Gokhale, Surendranath Banerjee, Pherozeshah Mehta, and M.G. Ranade were prominent Moderate leaders.
5. Methods of the Moderates
Moderates followed peaceful and constitutional methods to achieve political reforms.

• Submitting petitions and memorandums

• Passing resolutions in Congress sessions

• Public meetings and speeches

• Appeals to British Parliament

This approach is often described as ‘Prayer, Petition, and Protest’.

rows: Faith in British sense of justice and constitutional reform
Indianization of services, expansion of councils, economic relief

blocks.content: 6. Major Demands of the Moderates (Explained)
Moderates raised political, administrative, and economic demands.

• Expansion of Legislative Councils

• Indianisation of Civil Services

• Reduction of military expenditure

• Separation of judiciary from executive

• Reduction of land revenue

• Protection of Indian industries
7. Economic Critique: Drain of Wealth Theory
One of the greatest contributions of the Moderates was their economic critique of British rule.
Dadabhai Naoroji explained that India’s wealth was being drained to Britain through salaries, pensions, profits, and trade policies. This drain impoverished India and enriched Britain.
8. Achievements of the Moderate Phase
The Moderates succeeded in spreading political awareness, exposing British exploitation, and creating a national political platform.
9. Limitations of the Moderate Phase

items: A.O. Hume played a crucial role in the foundation of the Indian National Congress in 1885.
Dadabhai Naoroji authored the 'Drain of Wealth' theory, exposing British economic drain.
Lord Dufferin infamously referred to the INC as a 'microscopic minority'.
The political methods of the Moderate leaders are famously summarized as the '3 Ps': Prayer, Petition, and Protest.

blocks.content: Despite their contributions, Moderates failed to mobilise the masses. Their methods were slow and relied too heavily on British goodwill.
10. British Attitude towards the Moderates
Initially, the British tolerated the Congress. Later, they ignored its demands and adopted repressive measures.
11. Significance of the Period (1885–1905)
This phase trained Indian leaders, developed political consciousness, and prepared the ground for militant nationalism after 1905.
